newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, UPS talk under pressure from Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, UPS talk under pressure from Clinton.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Sunday urged the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service to reach an agreement ending a two-week strike that has crippled package deliveries throughout the country.
"It's clear that they're making progress," Clinton told reporters before boarding his helicopter to leave for vacation on Martha's Vineyard, off the Massachusetts coast.

"This strike is beginning to hurt not only the company but its employees and the people who depend on it, and I think they ought to redouble their efforts to settle the strike and they ought to do it today," the president said.
Deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey told reporters traveling with Clinton that he believed the two sides would either reach a settlement on Sunday or break off negotiations.
He said that if the parties could not reach agreement tonight Labor Secretary Alexis Herman would call for a recess in the talks to allow negotiators to get some rest.
In the absence of a settlement "she's going to send them home," Lindsey said.
In a conference call with more than 200 locals at 7 p.m. EDT (2300 GMT), Teamsters President Ron Carey said there was no agreement yet.
"We still don't have agreements on any major issue," he said, according to a Teamsters statement. Speaking in his regular weekly report on the strike, Carey urged his members to keep up the pressure.

"The strong support of our members and the public is the reason UPS is spending these hours talking with us," he said. "And it's that pressure that will get us a settlement that protects your future."

Earlier, Carey said on NBC television that marathon talks with UPS negotiators had made progress for the first time since negotiators hunkered down in a Washington hotel at the request of Herman on Thursday morning.

"There has been some movement," Carey said in explaining why he believed he was right not to put the company's previous so-called "last and final" offer to his 185,000 members for a vote as UPS executives had been urging.
"We are talking about the issues, and that to me is progress -- trying to see if we can find some areas of agreement and the talks are moving along," Carey said on NBC's "Meet the Press" program.
Company and union negotiators continued meeting on Sunday at a hotel across the street from the International Brotherhood of Teamsters headquarters.

UPS Chairman James Kelly, appearing on the same program, sounded an optimistic, though cautious, note, saying that negotiators were discussing "dozens and dozens of issues" but it was unclear when an agreement could be reached.
"The fact that we're continuing to talk is encouraging," Kelly said, repeating that the company would use replacement workers only as a last resort.

"We've been at make-or-break points a number of times before," Kelly told CNN later on Sunday. "Perhaps we're at another one right now." When asked if there was a chance that a settlement might be reached by midnight on Sunday, Kelly responded, "anything is possible."

The two sides have been in meetings since Thursday morning, taking a few brief sleep breaks along the way. Some times the parties meet face to face, other times with mediators and at other times with Herman.
Herman, who was credited by both sides with helping to keep the talks moving, was scheduled to fly to Los Angeles on Monday for a speaking engagement.

The walkout by drivers, loaders and sorters on Aug. 4 has crippled the nation's largest package delivery firm to the tune of an estimated $300 million a week in lost revenues and has cost UPS more than a half-billion dollars so far.
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to have their goods delivered.
UPS officials this week responded to a request by the Federal Reserve Board, sending officials a detailed analysis of the strike's impact on the company and the economy.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey has stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.
For its part, UPS has been seeking the withdrawal of its pension plan from its current multi-employer plan so it can set up a plan solely for Teamster members at UPS.
The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.
Clinton has been resisting calls by UPS and some business groups to seek an injunction under the Taft-Hartley Act that would temporarily halt the strike.
The strike is the largest since a three-day 1976 strike by 400,000 Teamster truck drivers, according to Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd.
